brief.head: Two traps for thinkers
brief.text: The first bar­rier to chang­ing your mind is con­ven­tional wis­dom and fa­mous names, Ajay Shah said, which he has re­sisted since child­hood. The sec­ond, ar­ro­gance, he finds harder. {055-C01}

brief.head: Protection backfires
brief.text: Cutting cus­toms du­ties makes im­ported in­puts cheaper and ex­ports more com­pet­i­tive, Ajay Shah said. The be­lief that ex­port­ing needs more pro­tec­tion­ism is “triv­ially and fac­tu­ally wrong”. {055-C02}

brief.head: The alumni effect
brief.text: Foreign firms often lead, Ajay Shah said, and their alumni then build do­mes­tic firms. Bangladesh’s gar­ment ex­ports grew that way, as Indian soft­ware did from Datamatics and TCS. {055-C05}

brief.head: No applause for upkeep
brief.text: Politicians and of­fi­cials enjoy an­nounce­ments and in­au­gu­ra­tions, Ajay Shah said. The quiet, hum­drum work of run­ning and reg­u­lat­ing as­sets wins no ap­plause, and is where the Indian state is weak­est. {055-C08}

brief.head: Bid for the subsidy
brief.text: Ashok Lahiri’s vi­a­bil­ity gap fund­ing, Ajay Shah said, lets bid­ders com­pete on how lit­tle sub­sidy they need for a road. The sub­sidy is then fixed, keep­ing the builder dis­ci­plined. {055-C10}

thought.who: John Maynard Keynes’s line, held up by Ajay Shah as an ideal he reaches too slowly

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah question a development faith
lead.head: Fibre delivered, the ports didn’t

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 55

body: Since the 1990s, build­ing roads, ports and air­ports has been treated in India as a sure bet for de­vel­op­ment. In this episode, Ajay Shah, who backed that bet, said it had come good only half­way.
Services ex­ports, he told Amit Varma, had worked “be­yond our wildest dreams”. The ports, high­ways, air­ports and rail­ways built to move goods did not.
“IT today is India’s big­gest in­dus­try. IT is what India does. IT is the only thing India has won in,” Shah said. {055-C06}
For goods, he said, “I just kept watch­ing the data and hop­ing and watch­ing the data and hop­ing.”
## The the­ory of the nineties
The the­ory came out of the 1990s, Shah ex­plained. Customs du­ties fell, rules on for­eign in­vest­ment changed, and ex­ports surged. Then the in­fra­struc­ture choked.

Half or more of world trade, Shah said, hap­pens in­side firms, which put each stage of pro­duc­tion wher­ever it is cheap­est. “We have no in­ter­est in na­tion­al­ity,” he said. “We just care that pro­duc­tion should be done in India.” {055-C03}

That meant mov­ing in­ter­me­di­ate goods cheaply to re­mote places where labour is cheap. So in­fra­struc­ture climbed onto the “high table of de­vel­op­ment strat­egy”, Shah said, be­fore catch­ing him­self an­thro­po­mor­phis­ing it.
## One suc­cess, one dis­ap­point­ment

For ser­vices, the the­ory worked. Once the state broke the tele­com mo­nop­oly, pri­vate firms laid fibre optic ca­bles into India, and ser­vices work spread from Bangalore and Hyderabad to dozens of smaller cities.

For goods, it did not. Shah took the ten years from 2012-13 to 2022-23, a win­dow that flat­ters India be­cause it in­cludes the post-pandemic boom. Even then, goods ex­ports grew 1.3 per cent a year in real dol­lars. {#real}

At that rate, he said, ex­ports dou­ble every 52 or 56 years, “which is just noth­ing”. Foreign di­rect in­vest­ment grew about 4 per cent a year in real terms. Global firms had not cho­sen India as a man­u­fac­tur­ing plat­form.
## Less bang for the buck
Shah gave four rea­sons why each rupee of in­fra­struc­ture now buys less, using a mea­sure econ­o­mists call the in­cre­men­tal cap­i­tal out­put ratio, or ICOR.

The best projects, such as the Golden Quadrilateral and JNPT, were done first. {055-C07} The state re­treated from pub­lic-private part­ner­ships to build­ing it­self. Project choice turned po­lit­i­cal. And of­fi­cials pre­fer launch­ing projects to run­ning them.
China, he said, had run into the same prob­lems, build­ing “roads to nowhere” and wast­ing tril­lions of dol­lars of poor people’s money.

Varma drew the les­son for pub­lic money. Every rupee the state spends, he noted from Shah’s book with Vijay Kelkar, *In Service of the Republic*, costs about three ru­pees of GDP, so spend­ing needs strong rea­sons.

Shah linked the ar­gu­ment to the pre­vi­ous episode, on ed­u­ca­tion. Lant Pritchett, he said, had been the lit­tle child say­ing the em­peror has no clothes, show­ing that pil­ing on years of school­ing did not de­liver de­vel­op­ment. The episode’s title echoes Pritchett’s paper.
The ques­tion that mat­ters, Shah said, is what most holds back firms from pro­duc­ing across India. “Infrastructure is prob­a­bly not the bind­ing con­straint today.” {055-C11}
That could change. If India fixed what­ever de­ters for­eign firms and in­vest­ment poured in, jammed ports and roads would make in­fra­struc­ture the choke point again.
Shah ad­mit­ted that the con­clu­sion cuts against his own past. “I was sup­port­ing that main par­a­digm in the nineties,” he said. “I’m just say­ing that my views have shifted.”

second.label: China’s build-out
second.head: The road less travelled
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how China’s infrastructure build wasted trillions

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on China’s roads to nowhere

body: China’s in­fra­struc­ture build was driven by cen­tral plan­ners and op­ti­mistic econ­o­mists who be­lieved that more in­fra­struc­ture would bring lots of good things, Ajay Shah said. Over time, po­lit­i­cal de­ci­sions took over, and roads were built with noth­ing at the other end. {055-S06}

In the short run, ev­ery­one was happy: there were con­struc­tion con­tracts, an­nounce­ments and rib­bon cut­tings. But mea­sured as in­cre­men­tal in­vest­ment against in­cre­men­tal GDP, each round bought less, and China’s ICOR kept get­ting worse.

By any rea­son­able ac­count, Shah said, China built too much in­fra­struc­ture and wasted tril­lions of dol­lars of the hard-won money of poor peo­ple. It is time, he ar­gued, for India to ask whether it should keep on doing more and more. {#india}

quote.text: There’s noth­ing at the other end. But vast money would be spent.

third.head: Sweet, made in USA

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the chikki of Ulhasnagar

body: Capitalism, Ajay Shah told Amit Varma, works by equal­is­ing dif­fer­ences: if wages, land or ma­te­ri­als are cheaper some­where, make the thing there and sell it where prices are high. {055-C04} Nobody in a good frame of mind, he said, would do low-end gar­ment work in Bombay.

So you would never make chikki in Lonavala, where real es­tate is ex­pen­sive. Was it made in China, Varma asked? Not China, Shah said, but Ulhasnagar. He had gone on a field trip to find out. {055-S08}
The punch­line, Shah said, was the an­swer he got: “Of course we don’t make it here. We make it in Ulhasnagar.”
Varma had a label ready. “So you could ac­tu­ally write on it made in USA,” he said. “USA stand­ing for Ulhasnagar Sweets Association.” {055-J02}

box.title: The paper behind the title
box.text: Lant Pritchett’s *Where Has All the Education Gone?* showed that pil­ing on years of school­ing did not de­liver de­vel­op­ment. Ajay Shah now turns the same scep­ti­cism on in­fra­struc­ture, and the episode bor­rows the paper’s ques­tion for its title. {055-R06}

sections.label: The theory
sections.head: Make it where it’s cheap
sections.caption: why infrastructure mattered
body: The case for in­fra­struc­ture, Ajay Shah said, be­gins in the 1990s. Customs du­ties came down, rules against for­eign in­vest­ment changed, and India got “a first surge of beau­ti­ful ex­ports growth”. {055-C02}
Then the in­fra­struc­ture choked, and it shot up everyone’s list of pri­or­i­ties.

The deeper rea­son lies in how global firms work. Half or more of global trade hap­pens within firms. A ball bear­ing goes to Brazil, an en­gine is made there, the en­gine comes to Madras, and the car is made in Madras and shipped out. A coun­try pros­pers, Shah said, by host­ing such pro­duc­tion chains, whether the firms are Indian or for­eign. {055-C03}
## Equalising dif­fer­ences

Shah of­fered a trick for un­der­stand­ing the world: cap­i­tal­ism works by equal­is­ing dif­fer­ences. Any gap in wages, land or raw ma­te­rial costs is a busi­ness op­por­tu­nity. You can­not house four­teen hun­dred mil­lion peo­ple in Bombay, he said, and its wages and real es­tate are too high for low-end gar­ment work any­way. {#bombay}

So the plan was for firms to put fac­to­ries in re­mote places where labour is cheap, and for roads, rail­ways, ports and air­ports to carry the ball bear­ing in and the re­sult out. That, Shah said, is how in­fra­struc­ture be­came cen­tral to India’s growth strat­egy.
~ It was not his idea, he stressed. In the 1990s, he said, the best and bright­est econ­o­mists un­der­stood the whole story, and the dream was “sky high”.

quote.text: Capitalism works by equal­is­ing dif­fer­ences. So if there’s a dif­fer­ence in a wage there’s a busi­ness op­por­tu­nity.

sections.label: The good story
sections.head: Getting out of the way
sections.caption: the telecom revolution
body: Telecom, Ajay Shah said, is “re­ally a great suc­cess story”. In the late 1990s the Vajpayee gov­ern­ment broke the Department of Telecom’s stran­gle­hold on tele­com pol­icy and opened the sec­tor to pri­vate and for­eign in­vest­ment. VSNL lost its mo­nop­oly on in­ter­na­tional tele­phony.

Private firms then ran fibre optic ca­bles to India, with land­ing sta­tions from the Middle East to Bombay and from Madras to Singapore. Users paid for it through their broad­band bills. “You don’t need gov­ern­ment money,” Shah said. “This should be about gov­ern­ment get­ting out of the way.” {055-S02}
Amit Varma re­mem­bered the ob­jec­tions of the time: tele­com was too im­por­tant, na­tional se­cu­rity was at stake, the state should con­trol it. People for­get those ar­gu­ments today, he said.
## Eight years late

Shah’s one com­plaint is tim­ing. The re­forms should have come on the same day as the cus­toms duty cuts, when India could im­port com­puter hard­ware and net­work switches. “We lost about eight years to get to ninety nine,” he said. {#eightyears}
By then, the ERNET project had al­ready seeded hun­dreds of peo­ple with UNIX and in­ter­net knowl­edge, on a pit­tance of a bud­get. {055-S01}
~ IT-ITES is now India’s big­gest in­dus­try, Shah said, with some three hun­dred to four hun­dred bil­lion dol­lars a year of fast-growing ser­vices ex­ports.

quote.text: So the full coun­try was rid­ing on 1.54 megabits a sec­ond.

sections.label: The bad story
sections.head: Watching and hoping
sections.caption: the goods that never took off
body: Ports, high­ways, air­ports and rail­ways were meant to do for goods what fibre did for ser­vices. A fac­tory in re­mote Vidarbha would make white cot­ton shirts and ship them to Europe. “But it didn’t work out,” Ajay Shah said.
Shah calls him­self an en­thu­si­ast for India, and year after year he watched the ex­port num­bers. “I just kept watch­ing the data and hop­ing and watch­ing the data and hop­ing.” {055-S05}
## A win­dow that flat­ters

To paint India at its best, he picked the ten years from 2012-13 to 2022-23. That win­dow in­cludes the surge in goods ex­ports after the pan­demic, when rich gov­ern­ments sent house­holds big fis­cal sup­port. Goods ex­ports grew 4 per cent a year in nom­i­nal dol­lars. {#goodsgrowth}
Taking out American in­fla­tion, about 2.7 per cent, left 1.3 per cent a year in real terms: a dou­bling every half-century or so. FDI grew at about 4 per cent a year in real terms.

Shah in­sisted on count­ing in con­stant US dol­lars, not ru­pees, since ex­change rates and in­fla­tion can cre­ate a money il­lu­sion, and goods such as iron ore are priced in dol­lars any­way. {#measure}
~ Global firms, his con­clu­sion ran, had not taken to India as a man­u­fac­tur­ing plat­form. “It’s time to of­fi­cially an­nounce that the goods ex­port story from India is not going well.”

quote.text: I’m an en­thu­si­ast for India. I just kept hop­ing that this will work.

sections.label: Diminishing returns
sections.head: Low-hanging fruit, all picked
sections.caption: the falling bang for the buck
body: Why does in­fra­struc­ture now give less bang for the buck? Ajay Shah gave four rea­sons, mea­sured by the in­cre­men­tal cap­i­tal out­put ratio, or ICOR.

First, di­min­ish­ing re­turns. The best projects, such as the Golden Quadrilateral, JNPT and the Delhi metro, get taken up first. {055-C07} “By the time you’re doing a metro in Nagpur, frankly, there’s very lit­tle use of a metro in Nagpur,” he said. {055-J04}

Second, after a “valiant and heroic at­tempt” at pub­lic-private part­ner­ships from 1991 to 2011 went badly, the state re­treated to build­ing things it­self, which costs more and is main­tained worse. The right an­swer, Shah said, was to learn to con­tract bet­ter. {055-C09}

Third, project choice turns po­lit­i­cal: a pow­er­ful person’s con­stituency, a re­li­gious site, a mar­ginal seat. Fourth, of­fi­cials pre­fer rib­bon cut­tings to the hum­drum work of run­ning as­sets.
## Digging ditches

Amit Varma added Frédéric Bastiat’s les­son about the seen and the un­seen. GDP counts state spend­ing as out­put, he said, so “you could just have an army of peo­ple dig­ging up ditches, fill­ing them up”, and GDP would keep going up. {055-C12}
The real ques­tion, he said, is what the money would have done if left with the tax­pay­ers it was taken from.
~ Varma’s own les­son, for in­di­vid­u­als and in­sti­tu­tions alike: don’t run away from hard prob­lems just be­cause they are hard.

quote.text: The right so­lu­tion is not for a gov­ern­ment to build stuff, but for a gov­ern­ment to do com­plex con­tracts with pri­vate per­sons

portraits.caption: Frédéric Bastiat
portraits.credit: Émile Desmaisons. Lithograph by Auguste-Hilaire Léveillé., public domain

sections.label: The core problem
sections.head: Find the choke point first
sections.caption: the binding constraint
body: There is no greater ques­tion for him, Ajay Shah said, than how India can put its pieces to­gether and be­come an ad­vanced econ­omy.

He set this episode be­side the pre­vi­ous one, on ed­u­ca­tion. Lant Pritchett, in his paper *Where Has All the Education Gone?*, was “the lit­tle child say­ing that the em­peror has no clothes”: years of school­ing had been piled on with­out de­liv­er­ing de­vel­op­ment. {055-J09}
Shah mocked the old faith that school­ing com­pa­ra­ble to the UK of 1947 would make India like the UK of 1947. {055-J03} Money, he ar­gued, should be pulled back until the fail­ure is di­ag­nosed.
## What holds firms back

Thinking on in­fra­struc­ture, he said, may be at the early stages of the same scep­ti­cism. The cen­tral ques­tion in de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics is what most holds back firms, Indian or for­eign, from lo­cat­ing pro­duc­tion across India. “Infrastructure is prob­a­bly not the bind­ing con­straint today.” {055-C11}

As a made-up ex­am­ple, he of­fered cap­i­tal con­trols and hos­tile tax­a­tion. Make India as hos­pitable as an OECD coun­try, and if a surge of FDI fol­lowed, full con­tainer ports and jammed roads would make in­fra­struc­ture the con­straint again.
~ “You must see those out­comes com­ing,” he added, “oth­er­wise your the­ory is wrong.”

quote.text: You should not con­tinue to put pub­lic money into things that are known to not work.

So the chal­lenge of being a state is the chal­lenge of high qual­ity, quiet hum­drum work where you don’t get ap­plause and you don’t score pro­pa­ganda points. And this is very dif­fi­cult in the Indian state.

p3.title: Field notes
p3.deck: A factory, an internet line, a coast and a port, and what each teaches

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s two days on a Bangalore factory floor
stories.head: The robot that fades your jeans
body: A cou­ple of months be­fore the episode, Ajay Shah spent two days at a blue jeans fac­tory be­long­ing to Arvind, on the out­skirts of Bangalore. He called them one of the great­est two days of his life.
The Arvind team had promised to show him one bad fac­tory and one good one. The good one, they told him, was the best blue jeans fac­tory in the coun­try. “I take their word for it,” Shah said.
It is a sin­gle fa­cil­ity with about 2,500 blue-collar work­ers, and it ex­ports ev­ery­thing it makes. {#jeans}

Inside, there is a con­stant march of ma­chines. India’s min­i­mum wages are high and ben­e­fits are manda­tory, so to stay com­pet­i­tive with Bangladesh and Vietnam, the firm keeps adding ma­chines one at a time, each jus­ti­fied by a hard-nosed in­ter­nal rate of re­turn cal­cu­la­tion.
Even the work of mak­ing new jeans look old and faded is done by a robot. This, Shah said, is the “in­ef­fi­cient cap­i­tal in­ten­sity” that micro­eco­nomics pre­dicts.

Then there were the shifts. “In the day shift, it’s al­most en­tirely women,” he said. Round the clock, prob­lems of phys­i­cal safety, trans­port and gov­ern­ment reg­u­la­tion take over, “and then it’s 100% men.” {055-S07}

Amit Varma saw a clas­sic il­lus­tra­tion of how min­i­mum wages harm the work­ers they are meant to help. Anyone whose work is val­ued below the min­i­mum loses the job: “in­stead of earn­ing X amount, they’re earn­ing zero, and ev­ery­body would agree that zero is worse.” {055-C13}
~ Shah, who loves field vis­its, asked lis­ten­ers to sug­gest more fac­to­ries for him to visit.
stories.why: A fac­tory floor shows how India’s labour rules shape firms. When the law makes work­ers ex­pen­sive, even a labour-intensive in­dus­try like jeans turns to ma­chines, and round-the-clock work be­comes a job for men only.
stories.postscript: Varma rec­om­mended his episode with the econ­o­mist Sowmya Dhanaraj, much of whose work is about women in fac­to­ries.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the jeans factory

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on India’s lone internet link of the early 1990s
stories.head: 1.54 megabits for all India
body: When Ajay Shah came back to India in the early 1990s, there was only one source of in­ter­net con­nec­tiv­ity in the coun­try: the National Centre for Software Technology, NCST.

Its head, S. Ramani, as Shah re­called, led a project called ERNET, a T1 line to the in­ter­net, which at the time sounded mind-blowing. {#t1} That meant 1.54 megabits a sec­ond for the whole of India. {055-S01}
On a pit­tance of a bud­get, ERNET seeded hun­dreds of peo­ple with UNIX and in­ter­net knowl­edge, in­clud­ing peo­ple the hosts know per­son­ally.

~ So when the tele­com mo­nop­oly ended later in the decade, that knowl­edge had al­ready spread across the coun­try. “I re­ally ad­mire and I’m grate­ful to the peo­ple in ERNET who cre­ated that be­gin­ning,” Shah said.
stories.why: Small, well-placed spend­ing on knowl­edge can mat­ter enor­mously. ERNET built the human cap­i­tal for the ser­vices boom be­fore the band­width ar­rived, so that when pri­vate fibre came, peo­ple across India were ready to use it.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on ERNET’s single line

stories.kicker: A founder’s account of how services work spread
stories.head: Crawling up the coast
body: Services work did not stay in Bombay, Ajay Shah said. It went to Bangalore, Hyderabad, Pune and Madras, and to dozens of smaller cities.

The founder of Mphasis once told him how. “Today we are crawl­ing up the coast of Andhra Pradesh and Orissa,” the founder said, pick­ing towns of five to ten lakh peo­ple: “we put a build­ing there, we hire two thou­sand peo­ple there, and we are up and run­ning.” {055-S03}

It starts with call cen­tres, where the firm pol­ishes recruits’ ac­cent and gram­mar, and moves up to soft­ware. The worker stays close to her home in­stead of mi­grat­ing, and fibre optic ca­bles carry her work around the world.
~ This is equal­is­ing dif­fer­ences at work, Shah said: cheap labour in Vijayawada is cheaper than in Bangalore, so why build one more fa­cil­ity in Bangalore? {#vijayawada}

quote.text: Living close to her home, not need­ing to leave home and mi­grate.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Mphasis on the coast

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a 1990s port design
stories.head: Competition docks at JNPT
body: In the 1990s, Ajay Shah said, there was won­der­ful work on pro-competitive frame­works for JNPT, then India’s big­gest con­tainer ter­mi­nal, in Bombay.
The gov­ern­ment did not hand the port to one pri­vate op­er­a­tor as a sin­gle pub­lic-private part­ner­ship. Instead it or­gan­ised JNPT as three com­pet­ing ter­mi­nals in one port. {055-S04}

One ter­mi­nal stayed with the gov­ern­ment, so that costs could be mea­sured and prices bench­marked. The other two were con­tracted out to two dif­fer­ent pri­vate ven­dors. The re­sult, Shah said, was vig­or­ous com­pe­ti­tion.

~ He counts JNPT, with the Golden Quadrilateral and the Bombay and Delhi air­ports, among the burn­ing pri­or­i­ties of the 1990s: the projects with the high­est bang for the buck, taken up first. {055-C07}

quote.text: Sadly some of that level of bril­liance in pol­icy doesn’t hap­pen in many later episodes in Indian in­fra­struc­ture.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on JNPT’s three terminals

quiz.q: Which ratio did Ajay Shah use to show infrastructure’s falling bang for the buck?
quiz.a: ICOR, the in­cre­men­tal cap­i­tal out­put ratio, com­par­ing extra cap­i­tal with extra out­put.

quiz.q: How did the government design JNPT so that one port would have real competition?
quiz.a: As three com­pet­ing ter­mi­nals: one gov­ern­ment-run, two con­tracted to dif­fer­ent pri­vate ven­dors.

quiz.q: In Ashok Lahiri’s viability gap funding, what do bidders compete over in the reverse auction?
quiz.a: How lit­tle sub­sidy they need; the sub­sidy is then fixed for the builder.

quiz.q: Which economist’s line about changing your mind when facts change did Ajay Shah hold up?
quiz.a: John Maynard Keynes’s; Shah ad­mit­ted he him­self changes his mind too slowly.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 55. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Frédéric Bastiat (Émile Desmaisons. Lithograph by Auguste-Hilaire Léveillé., public domain); Atal Bihari Vajpayee (Government of India, GODL-India); Vivian Gornick (librairie mollat, CC BY 3.0); Paul Graham (Sarah Harlin, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Young Rural Women in India Chase Big-City Dreams
shelf.creator: Ellen Barry
shelf.why: Ajay sees firms and ex­ports as the heart and soul of the Indian story.

shelf.title: Follow-Up: A New Ending in Tale of Young Woman From Rural India
shelf.creator: Ellen Barry
shelf.why: It con­tin­ues the story of one of the young women from the orig­i­nal Tirupur piece.

shelf.title: The Odd Woman and the City
shelf.creator: Vivian Gornick
shelf.why: He fell in love with Gornick’s writ­ing and says it made him want to write.

shelf.title: Sowmya Dhanaraj Is Making a Difference (Episode 380 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: One of Amit’s ten favourite episodes: econ­o­mist Sowmya Dhanaraj, whose par­ents were fac­tory work­ers and whose mother sold tea on the Coimbatore high­way, ques­tions re­ceived wis­dom from lived Indian re­al­ity rather than im­ported frame­works.

shelf.title: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s most pop­u­lar Seen and the Unseen episode, a con­ver­sa­tion with Shrayana Bhattacharya (who gave him the ‘anti-uncle’ label) on the eco­nomic and so­cial lives of Indian women.

shelf.title: Where Has All the Education Gone?
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett
shelf.why: Pritchett’s cross-country anal­y­sis find­ing that ex­pand­ing school­ing pro­duced es­sen­tially zero growth, which Ajay calls one of the most im­por­tant pa­pers in de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: Bastiat’s bro­ken-window para­ble, which teaches you to look past a policy’s vis­i­ble ef­fect to its un­seen costs and in­tro­duced op­por­tu­nity cost decades be­fore the term ex­isted.

shelf.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Explains that politi­cians and bu­reau­crats re­spond to in­cen­tives like ev­ery­one else, so the state is no benev­o­lent beast and gov­ern­ment fail­ure is far more com­mon than mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Paul Graham’s two-axis map of thinkers (con­ven­tional or in­de­pen­dent, pas­sive or ag­gres­sive) that sin­gles out the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded as the loud­est voices and the real ob­sta­cle to new ideas.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Education (Episode 54)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Decades of both hosts’ think­ing on ed­u­ca­tion packed into about an hour, an episode Amit is proud of.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Chess (Episode 52)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A syn­the­sis of Amit’s knowl­edge of and en­thu­si­asm for chess, walk­ing through every world cham­pion up to Ding and the role of com­put­ers in the game.

shelf.title: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s case that in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion is the en­gine of growth: com­pet­ing with the world forces firms to im­port best prac­tices and raise their game, and the gains spread through the econ­omy.

shelf.title: How Family Firms Evolve (Episode 34) and From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37) of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Original think­ing from Ajay on how Indian firms evolved over 30 years and how they should ma­ture: from fam­ily con­trol to dis­persed share­hold­ing, a pow­er­ful board and a man­age­ment team ac­count­able to it.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: Public Finance at XKDR Forum
shelf.creator: XKDR Forum
shelf.why: XKDR Forum’s re­search pro­gramme on pub­lic fi­nance and gov­ern­ment con­tract­ing, stud­ied field by field to draw gen­eral lessons.

laughs.text: Amit opens by not­ing that Ajay is wear­ing a sparkling white kurta (‘the Sanskari look’) with an ant climb­ing up his col­lar. Later he in­ter­rupts Ajay’s ac­count of being a life­long free thinker to re­port that the ant is now on his neck, then says: ‘Anyway, con­tinue.’
Ajay says the Lonavala chikki is made in Ulhasnagar. Amit: ‘So you could ac­tu­ally write on it made in USA. USA stand­ing for Ulhasnagar Sweets Association.’
Ajay on di­min­ish­ing re­turns: a Delhi metro is valu­able, but ‘by the time you’re doing a metro in Nagpur, you know, frankly, there’s very lit­tle use of a metro in Nagpur.’

After de­scrib­ing in­fra­struc­ture climb­ing onto the ‘high table of de­vel­op­ment strategy’ and declar­ing it­self top pri­or­ity, Ajay catches him­self: ‘Now I’m an­thro­po­mor­phiz­ing a block named in­fra­struc­ture.’
John Maynard Keynes: ‘When the facts change, I change my mind, and what do you do, sir?’ Ajay holds this up as the ideal and ad­mits he changes his mind too slowly.

Ajay lists the econ­o­mists he ad­mires but ar­gues with: Larry Summers, Marty Feldstein, Lant Pritchett and Jeff Hammer. He treats them as a kick-off for an ar­gu­ment: ‘Puny lit­tle me is going to argue about this with a great per­son.’
Paul Graham’s phrase ‘ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded’, from The Four Quadrants of Conformism, which Amit uses for the peo­ple who push back on any­one ques­tion­ing a con­sen­sus.

The Emperor’s New Clothes: Ajay casts Lant Pritchett as ‘the lit­tle child say­ing that the em­peror has no clothes’ with his paper ‘Where Has All the Education Gone?’, which gives this episode its title.
Frédéric Bastiat and ‘the seen and the unseen’: Amit in­vokes Bastiat to argue that state spend­ing hides a large op­por­tu­nity cost.
